judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The footer image is the 'Ministério da Cultura' logo (text plus the Brazilian flag mark), a standalone img with alt="", not inside a link and with no caption. I looked for a technique that would make it pass: the snapshot has no text anywhere on the page naming the Ministério da Cultura (only an Ouvidoria link whose href points to gov.br/cultura, and an 'SAv/MinC' menu abbreviation, neither of which conveys the affiliation). A logo that states the institution's affiliation is informative, not ambience, so hiding it removes information sighted users get. The live page still has alt="" on it. The finding holds.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: 'A Cinemateca' is the top-level item of the fixed main navigation, an a href="#" that opens a nested sub-menu (A Cinemateca, Instalações, Transparência, Notícias, SAC, SAv/MinC). Its text names the section that its sub-menu holds, and the nested list in the nav gives the programmatic context, so its purpose is determinable. The claim that the text is 'an address, not a purpose' does not describe a 2.4.4 failure. Using a fake link with href="#" as a disclosure control, with no button role or aria-expanded, is a 4.1.2 concern, not a link-purpose one.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: 'SAv/MinC' is a sub-menu link under the 'A Cinemateca' nav section. It goes to /a-cinemateca/sav-minc/, whose title is 'SAv/MinC - Cinemateca Brasileira', a page about the Ministry of Culture's Secretaria do Audiovisual. The link text names its destination exactly. It is an acronym that is well known in the Brazilian film sector, and it is no more cryptic to a screen-reader user than to anyone else. 2.4.4 does not require abbreviations in link text to be expanded (that is 3.1.4, Level AAA), so it is being applied more strictly than WCAG requires.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the desktop variant of an archival black-and-white still (a man seated on a TV set, seen past a woman's shoulder). It illustrates the 'Assessoria de Imprensa' section and has no caption and no role in the content, so it is ambience imagery that alt="" handles correctly. The only text in it is a partly visible name on a studio monitor, which reads roughly 'JECE VALA…' (likely Jece Valadão), not 'JACK VULCAN' as the finding says. That incidental, cropped text in the photo is not information the page conveys. The finding misreads the image and treats a decorative photo as informative.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the large hero photo of the Fale Conosco page: a film still of the comedian Oscarito holding a phone in front of a prop dial. It has no caption and only sets the 'contact us' mood. The words on the prop dial (actually ARTUR, SANSÃO, ELESTAL, C.C.P., COFAP, BOTECO, which the finding mis-transcribes) are incidental scenery in the picture, not information the page means to convey, so alt="" is acceptable decorative treatment under 1.1.1. The finding's claim that those labels are missing content does not hold.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The contact form's 'Telefone' field (input type="tel" name="telefone", named only by its placeholder) collects the user's own phone number, which is a purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list (tel). It has no autocomplete attribute. Its siblings show the site knows the technique: the email field has autocomplete="email", and the name field has the invalid autocomplete="nome". I checked whether type="tel" could count as identifying the purpose. It only declares the data format, not that this is the user's telephone, and H98 (autocomplete) is the sufficient technique. The live page is unchanged, so 1.3.5 fails as reported.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: 'Acervo' is a top-level item of the main navigation, an a href="#" that opens a nested sub-menu (Acervo, Biblioteca, Base de Dados, Publicações, Depósitos e Doações, BCC). On a cinematheque's site, 'Acervo' (the collection) clearly names the section, and the nested list gives the programmatic context, so the claim that nothing tells where it goes is wrong. Any problem with the href="#" disclosure pattern belongs under 4.1.2, not 2.4.4.
